messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Curriculum Designer
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion, Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Vignette:
Malia, a 66-year-old divorced woman of Oceanic background who worked for many years as a curriculum designer, came to describe her wartime experience in the language of fragments. She said that what happened still did not feel fully believable to her, as if it belonged to someone else’s life, or to a story so extreme that it was difficult to accept it had happened to her at all. When she tried to speak about it, she often knew the facts but could not find the words to hold them together. The memories arrived in disconnected pieces: a flash of sky, the thudding approach of a helicopter, the sense of people around her looking to someone else for orders, and her own body bracing before she could think. Even now, the event came back uninvited, sometimes in the middle of ordinary moments, with no warning beyond a sudden intrusion of the scene into her mind.

She linked the trauma to combat conditions in which she had felt trapped beneath other people’s power and decisions. What stayed with her most vividly was not a single complete narrative but the experience of being in a situation where someone else held authority over whether she and others were safe. The imbalance of power was what made certain moments in the memory so potent for her now. She said that when she finds herself around people who seem to have control over her options, she immediately feels the old tightening in her chest and wants to get away. She has come to watch for that feeling carefully in everyday life, and she dislikes how quickly it can appear even in settings that are objectively ordinary. Helicopter or aircraft sounds are especially jarring for her. The sound can catch her off guard outdoors or even when she is near a road and hears a low mechanical roar overhead, and in that instant she is back in the sensory world of the event, alert and tense before she has time to orient herself.

Over the years, Malia developed habits meant to keep those reactions from overwhelming her. She began avoiding going out unless she had to, gradually shaping her days around what she believed would be the least exposing route and the shortest possible time away from home. When she does leave, she makes sure to stay close to an exit, even in places she knows well, positioning herself where she can leave quickly if she feels trapped. In meetings, at appointments, or even in a restaurant, she scans for doors and calculates how to reach them. She has also tried not to allow herself to feel strong emotion, telling herself that if she starts to feel too much, the memories will become harder to contain. She learned to keep conversations contained and to move on quickly when topics approached anything that stirred up fear, anger, or sadness. Those efforts have narrowed her life in practical ways. As a divorced woman living alone, she has grown increasingly reluctant to make plans that involve unfamiliar places or crowded environments, and the shrinking of her routine has left her feeling increasingly apart from other people.

Malia’s current work as a curriculum designer has remained meaningful to her, but even there she notices the same alertness. In staff meetings and consultations, she is especially uneasy when a supervisor or senior administrator speaks in a way that reminds her of being under someone else’s control. She may focus on the door, sit upright, and rehearse in her mind how she would leave if needed. She worries quietly that she cannot trust herself to do the right thing if pressure rises too quickly. That self-doubt has become part of how she sees herself now: someone who cannot rely on her own judgment when a situation becomes too charged. She also experiences herself as set apart from others, as though the version of her life shaped by combat has left her on the edge of ordinary social ease. Even when she is with colleagues or family, she can feel as if she is standing slightly outside the group, watching rather than belonging.

She sought help after noticing how much her world had narrowed and how often she was living on guard. The sudden memory intrusions, the reactions to helicopter sounds, and the dread of being in places where she cannot quickly leave had become harder to manage, especially as she became more aware of how much she was missing by staying in. What brought her to treatment was not a single crisis but the accumulation of years spent bracing herself, avoiding strong feeling, and arranging her days around exits and escape routes. She came hoping to feel less isolated and less controlled by the old fear, though what she feared most was that if she let her guard drop, the memory would return in full and she would again be left with the same helplessness she remembers from the event itself.
